mainTopic: The closing laws of מסכת מגילה: blessing over the open ספר תורה, proper handling and honor of the ספר תורה, and studying each festival's laws in its season.
overview: This amud, the last of מסכת מגילה, opens by finishing a discussion from the previous amud. רבי זירא described the practice step by step instead of saying 'הלכה כרבי יהודה', because some people had switched the names in the ברייתא. The גמרא then brings that ברייתא. רבי מאיר says the reader closes the scroll before the ברכה, so people will not think the ברכות are written in the Torah. רבי יהודה says the reader may bless over the open scroll, and that is the הלכה. Next comes a series of practical rules about handling a ספר תורה: how to roll and tighten it, why the greatest person present should do גלילה, and why one should not hold the bare parchment. In between, רבי יוחנן teaches when one may rely on a בת קול. He also applies a harsh פסוק to reading without a tune, and אביי objects and reapplies it to scholars who quarrel. The amud ends with the משנה's teaching that each יום טוב's portion is read in its own time, and משה's תקנה to study each festival's הלכות on that festival.

steps.title: Why the ruling had to be stated: some reversed the names
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers an earlier question. רבי זירא had to say clearly which opinion is the הלכה because some people had swapped the names in the ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because there are those who reverse them (the names of the תנאים).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a discussion from the previous amud. It explains why רבי זירא spelled out the practice step by step instead of simply saying 'the הלכה follows רבי יהודה.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some versions of the ברייתא gave רבי מאיר's view to רבי יהודה, and רבי יהודה's view to רבי מאיר. So saying only 'the הלכה follows רבי יהודה' could be confusing. That is why רבי זירא spelled out the actual practice.

keyTerms.meaning: They reverse or switch (here: switch the names of who said what)
Because

phrases.english: Because there are those who reverse them.
phrases.notes: 'Them' refers to the names of רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה in the ברייתא that follows.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised on the previous amud: why רבי זירא described the practice instead of saying 'הלכה כרבי יהודה'.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Textual: the attribution in the ברייתא was disputed, so an explicit ruling was necessary.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי זירא could simply have said 'the הלכה follows רבי יהודה' instead of describing each action.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because some versions switched the names, the practice had to be stated clearly to avoid confusion.

steps.title: The ברייתא: close the scroll before the blessing, or bless while it is open?
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא records a מחלוקת. רבי מאיר says to open the scroll, close it, say the ברכה, then reopen and read. רבי יהודה says to open the scroll, say the ברכה, and read without closing it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: He opens the scroll and looks at the place. He rolls it closed and says the blessing. Then he opens it again and reads. These are the words of רבי מאיר. רבי יהודה says: He opens it, looks, says the blessing, and reads.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא in which two תנאים disagree about how to handle the scroll when saying the ברכה over the Torah reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions agree that the reader first opens the scroll to find his place. They disagree on one point only. רבי מאיר wants the scroll closed while the ברכה is said. רבי יהודה lets the reader say the ברכה over the open scroll.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught; introduces a ברייתא
He opens the scroll and looks at the place he will read
He rolls the scroll closed
He says the ברכה
And he opens it again

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי מאיר skips finding the place. He also opens the scroll and looks first. His only extra step is closing it before the ברכה and opening it again afterward.
steps.whyThisMatters: Step 6 rules that the הלכה follows רבי יהודה's practice. That is why the common practice is to say the ברכה over an open scroll.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
He opens and looks, rolls it closed and blesses,
and then opens it again and reads.
These are the words of Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
He opens and looks, and blesses and reads.
phrases.notes: He does not close the scroll in between.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Quotes the ברייתא whose names were said to be reversed in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: close the scroll before the ברכה, then reopen it to read. רבי יהודה: say the ברכה over the open scroll and read.

steps.title: What is רבי מאיר's reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי מאיר requires closing the scroll before the ברכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of רבי מאיר?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reasoning behind רבי מאיר's extra step. This line sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Closing and reopening the scroll is extra work, so it needs a reason. The question is not an attack. It is a request to explain the logic.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?

phrases.english: What is the reason of Rabbi Meir?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the reasoning behind רבי מאיר's view in the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why must the scroll be closed while the ברכה is said?

steps.title: רבי מאיר's reason: people might think the blessings are written in the Torah
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר's reason matches עולא's rule. The reader may not help the translator so people won't think the תרגום is written in the Torah. In the same way, the scroll is closed during the ברכה so people won't think the ברכות are written in it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It follows עולא, for עולא said: Why did they say that the one reading the Torah should not help the translator? So that people should not say the translation is written in the Torah. Here too: so that people should not say the blessings are written in the Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by comparing this case to a known rule of עולא about the reader and the translator (מתורגמן).
steps.deeperAnalysis: עולא's concern is that words spoken by the reader, who stands over the scroll, may be mistaken for part of the written Torah. רבי מאיר applies the same concern to the ברכות. If the reader says them over an open scroll, people may think they are being read from it, so he closes the scroll.

keyTerms.meaning: עולא, an אמורא whose rule is used here
The translator who said the Aramaic translation aloud during the reading
The Aramaic translation of the Torah reading
So that people should not say (mistakenly think)
Here too; applies the same logic to this case

phrases.english: It is like Ulla, for Ulla said:
For what reason did they say
that the one reading the Torah should not assist the translator?
So that people should not say
that the translation is written in the Torah.
Here too:
so that people should not say
that the blessings are written in the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי מאיר is concerned, as עולא is, that people will think words said over the scroll are part of the written Torah. So he closes the scroll during the ברכות.

steps.title: רבי יהודה's view: the translation can be confused with the text, the blessings cannot
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה distinguishes the two cases. The תרגום could be mistaken for the Torah text, but the ברכות could not, so the scroll may stay open.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהודה holds: With the translation, there is room to make a mistake. With the blessings, there is no room to make a mistake.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רבי יהודה does not accept the comparison to עולא's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תרגום follows the verses closely, so people could think it is also written in the scroll. The ברכות are clearly a separate formula that every reader says each time. No one will think they come from the Torah text, so there is no need to close the scroll.

keyTerms.meaning: There is room to make a mistake
There is no room to make a mistake
The ברכות said before and after the reading

steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר closes the scroll during the ברכה so people won't think the ברכות are written in the Torah, based on עולא's rule about the תרגום. רבי יהודה says no one will confuse the ברכות with the Torah text, so the reader may bless over the open scroll. The הלכה follows רבי יהודה.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehuda?
With the translation, there is room to err;
with the blessings, there is no room to err.
phrases.notes: Everyone knows the ברכות are a set formula said by each reader, not verses from the scroll.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the comparison made in step 4, explaining why רבי יהודה does not apply עולא's concern to the ברכות.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction between cases (חילוק): the תרגום can be confused with the text, the ברכות cannot.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: עולא's concern about the תרגום should apply equally to the ברכות.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברכות are obviously separate from the Torah text, so no one will be misled, and the scroll may remain open.

steps.title: The final ruling: open, look, bless, read
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא in the name of רב מתנה rules that the reader opens the scroll, looks at the place, says the ברכה and reads, without closing it in between.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said in the name of רב מתנה: The הלכה is that he opens the scroll, looks at the place, says the ברכה, and reads.
steps.whatsHappening: After the מחלוקת between רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה, the גמרא now gives the practical הלכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is no step of closing the scroll in this list. So the ruling matches רבי יהודה, who said the scroll may stay open during the ברכה. Notice that רבי זירא describes the actions one by one and does not name either תנא. The next step asks about exactly that.

keyTerms.meaning: The final practical law
He opens the scroll and looks at the place he will read
He says the ברכה and reads

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practice in shul today. The בעל קריאה opens the ספר תורה and shows the place, and the עולה says the ברכה while the scroll is open. Many people turn their face slightly to the side while saying it.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא אָמַר רַב מַתְנָה:
phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said in the name of Rav Mattana:
The law is: he opens the scroll and looks at the place
phrases.notes: There is no closing step. That is רבי יהודה's view.

phrases.english: and he says the blessing and reads.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא אָמַר רַב מַתְנָה: הֲלָכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the מחלוקת between רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Open the scroll, look, say the ברכה and read, without closing the scroll in between.

steps.title: Why not just name רבי יהודה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי זירא spelled out the actions instead of simply saying the הלכה follows רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him just say: the הלכה follows רבי יהודה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about the wording of the ruling. This question sets up the answer that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally an אמורא rules briefly by naming the תנא whose view is followed. Writing out every action looks like extra words, so the גמרא wants to know why it was done. The question is about wording, not about what the הלכה is.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Let him say', meaning he should have said it this simpler way
'The law follows...', the usual short way to give a ruling

phrases.english: So let him say: The law follows Rabbi Yehuda!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions how the ruling in step 6 was worded.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the long description instead of the short formula 'הלכה כרבי יהודה'?

steps.title: Some people swapped the names
steps.stepSummary: Some people had reversed which view belongs to רבי מאיר and which to רבי יהודה. So naming a תנא would be unclear, and describing the actions avoids any mistake.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because there are people who reverse the names.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רבי זירא described the actions: some versions of the ברייתא swapped the two names.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If someone held the swapped version, the words 'הלכה כרבי יהודה' would lead him to close the scroll, which is the wrong practice. Describing the actual steps gives one clear practice that works no matter which version a person has.

keyTerms.meaning: They reverse them, meaning they swap the names of the two תנאים
Because...

steps.confusionAlert: This is the same point summarized in Step 1. Here we see the actual words of the גמרא. It is not a new argument.
steps.whatToRemember: When the names in a ברייתא are in doubt, an אמורא may give the ruling by describing the practice instead of naming a תנא.

phrases.english: Because there are those who reverse the names.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording question of step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the wording by pointing to a doubt about which name goes with which view.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He could have just written 'the הלכה follows רבי יהודה.'
steps.terutzMaskana: Because some people swapped the names, only describing the actions makes the ruling clear.

steps.title: The לוחות and בימות have no holiness
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא in the name of רב מתנה rules that the לוחות and the בימות have no קדושה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said in the name of רב מתנה: The לוחות and the בימות have no קדושה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new, separate ruling from the same pair of אמוראים. It is about items used together with the ספר תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sefaria explains the לוחות as the empty margins of the scroll. Other מפרשים explain them as boards connected to the scroll. The בימות are the platforms where the Torah is read. Even though these are used right next to the ספר תורה, they do not have the קדושה of the scroll itself.

keyTerms.meaning: Boards. Sefaria explains them as the blank margins of the scroll.
Platforms from which the Torah is read
Holiness, a sacred status that brings rules for handling and disposal

steps.whyThisMatters: This helps set the boundary between the ספר תורה itself and the items around it. That boundary matters for questions like how the items are treated and how they may be disposed of.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא אָמַר רַב מַתְנָה:
phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said in the name of Rav Mattana:
The boards and the platforms
do not have any sanctity.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא אָמַר רַב מַתְנָה: הַלּוּחוֹת וְהַבִּימוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ruling from the same אמוראים. It is not part of the ברכה discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The לוחות and בימות have no קדושה.

steps.title: Close the scroll on a seam
steps.stepSummary: רבי שפטיה in the name of רבי יוחנן rules that when you close a ספר תורה, you should stop so that a seam between two sheets sits between the rollers.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שפטיה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Someone who rolls up a ספר תורה should set it so that it closes on the seam.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new practical rule about closing a ספר תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the scroll is pulled or tied too tightly, the strain falls on the part between the two rollers. When a seam is there, it will come apart at the stitching, which can be sewn again, and not tear through the written words.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone who rolls up the Torah scroll
Seam, the stitching where two sheets of parchment are joined
That he should set it in place

steps.whyThisMatters: This is why the גולל in shul tries to close the ספר תורה with a seam in the middle.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁפַטְיָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shefatya said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan:
One who rolls up a Torah scroll
needs to set it so it closes on the seam.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁפַטְיָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: הַגּוֹלֵל סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic about the proper way to handle a ספר תורה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Close the ספר תורה so that a seam sits between the two rollers.

steps.title: Roll from the outside, not the inside
steps.stepSummary: רבי שפטיה in the name of רבי יוחנן adds that the scroll should be rolled from the outside and not from the inside.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי שפטיה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Someone rolling a ספר תורה rolls it from the outside, and does not roll it from the inside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second rule from the same speakers. It is about which direction to turn the scroll when rolling it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Following Sefaria: 'From the outside' means turning the farther roller toward yourself. 'From the inside' means pushing the nearer roller away from yourself. If you push away and lose control, the scroll could roll off onto the floor. Rolling toward yourself keeps it safe.

keyTerms.meaning: From the outside: turning the far roller toward yourself
From the inside: pushing the near roller away from yourself
He rolls it

steps.whatToRemember: Three practical rules for handling a ספר תורה: the לוחות and בימות have no קדושה, close the scroll on a seam, and roll it toward yourself so it cannot fall.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁפַטְיָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Shefatya said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan:
One who rolls a Torah scroll
rolls it from the outside,
phrases.notes: Turning the far roller toward himself.

phrases.english: and does not roll it from the inside.
phrases.notes: Pushing the near roller away risks the scroll falling.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁפַטְיָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: הַגּוֹלֵל סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second rule from the same speakers on the same topic of rolling a ספר תורה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Roll the ספר תורה from the outside, toward yourself, and not from the inside.

steps.title: Tightening the scroll from the inside
steps.stepSummary: After finding the right place, you tighten the ספר תורה from the inside, not from the outside.
steps.simpleTranslation: And when he tightens it, he tightens it from the inside, and does not tighten it from the outside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רבי שפטיה's rules about handling the ספר תורה. Once the scroll is rolled to the right place, it should be tightened from the inside.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 dealt with rolling the scroll. This line deals with the final tightening. Turning the roller closest to you keeps your arms from stretching over the writing, so the צבור can still see the text.

keyTerms.meaning: He tightens it (pulls the scroll snug)
From the inside (the roller nearest you)
From the outside (the roller farther from you)

phrases.english: And when he tightens it
he tightens it from the inside,
phrases.notes: By turning the roller closest to himself.

phrases.english: and does not tighten it from the outside.
phrases.notes: So his arms do not block the community's view of the text.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same רבי שפטיה rule about handling the scroll, adding how to tighten it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Tighten the ספר תורה from the inside, not from the outside.

steps.title: The greatest of the readers rolls the Torah
steps.stepSummary: When ten people read from the Torah, the greatest among them should do the גלילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי שפטיה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: When ten people read from the Torah, the greatest among them rolls the ספר תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: A new ruling from רבי שפטיה in the name of רבי יוחנן. The honor of rolling the Torah goes to the most distinguished of those who read.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This tells us that גלילה is not a minor job. It is the top honor, so it belongs to the greatest person present. The next step explains why.

keyTerms.meaning: Ten who read (from the Torah)
The greatest among them
Rolls (closes) the scroll; one who does גלילה

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁפַטְיָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Shefatya said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
Ten who read from the Torah,
the greatest among them rolls the Torah scroll.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁפַטְיָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next ruling in the same series of statements from רבי שפטיה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The greatest of the ten readers does the גלילה.

steps.title: The roller earns the reward of all the readers
steps.stepSummary: The גולל takes the reward of all of them, as רבי יהושע בן לוי taught.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who rolls it takes the reward of all of them, as רבי יהושע בן לוי said: When ten read from the Torah, the one who rolls the ספר תורה received the reward of all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן's statement continues: the one who rolls the Torah takes the reward of all the readers. A teaching of רבי יהושע בן לוי is brought to back this up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the גולל earns so much reward, his job is the biggest honor. That is why it goes to the greatest person. The statement of רבי יהושע בן לוי is the source for this claim about reward.

keyTerms.meaning: The reward of all of them
Received
As he said (introduces a supporting source)

phrases.english: The one who rolls it takes the reward of all of them,
as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
Ten who read from the Torah,

phrases.aramaic: הַגּוֹלֵל סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה קִיבֵּל שְׂכַר כּוּלָּן.
phrases.english: the one who rolls the Torah scroll received the reward of all of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason behind step 13 and supports it with an earlier teaching.
steps.raayaObject: That the greatest should roll, since the גולל's reward is so great.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יהושע בן לוי: the גולל receives the reward of all ten readers.

steps.title: Do the others lose their reward?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the wording: could the roller really take away everyone else's reward?
steps.simpleTranslation: The reward of all of them — could that enter your mind?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the wording "שכר כולן". Taken literally, it sounds as if the readers lose their reward to the roller.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Why should the ten readers lose what they earned just because someone else rolled the scroll? That would make no sense. So the literal wording cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: Could it enter your mind? (this cannot be meant literally)

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying the גולל gets less. It is only rejecting the idea that the readers lose their own reward.

phrases.english: The reward of all of them — can that enter your mind?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the literal wording of the statement in step 14.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Read literally, it means the readers forfeit their reward to the גולל, which is unreasonable.

steps.title: A reward equal to all of them
steps.stepSummary: The wording is fixed: the גולל receives a reward equal to the reward of all of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: he received a reward equal to all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא corrects the wording. The roller gets a reward as big as all the readers' rewards combined, and they keep their own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fix changes "the reward of all" to "a reward equal to all." Nobody loses anything. The גולל simply earns a very large reward of his own, which is why the job is the greatest honor.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, say (a correction of the wording)
Equal to all of them

steps.whatToRemember: גלילה is a great honor. The גולל earns a reward equal to all the readers combined, so the greatest person present should do it.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
he received a reward equal to all of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 15 by changing the wording.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The roller takes away the readers' reward.
steps.terutzMaskana: The roller receives his own reward, equal in size to all of theirs combined.

steps.title: A source for relying on a בת קול
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן derives from a פסוק in ישעיהו that a person may use a בת קול as a guide.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי שפטיה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: From where do we know that one may make use of a בת קול? As it says: "And your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying."
steps.whatsHappening: Another ruling in the series. רבי יוחנן brings a פסוק showing that a person may be guided by a voice he happens to hear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here a בת קול means a chance voice that seems to answer what a person is unsure about. The פסוק describes hearing a word "behind you" that shows the way. That is the source for treating such a voice as a sign.

keyTerms.meaning: From where (do we know)?
One may make use of
A heavenly echo; a chance voice taken as a sign
As it is said (introduces a פסוק)

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁפַטְיָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Shefatya said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
From where do we know that one may make use of a Divine Voice?
As it is said: "And your ears shall hear a word
behind you, saying".
phrases.notes: ישעיהו ל:כא. It continues: "This is the way, walk in it."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁפַטְיָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִנַּיִן שֶׁמִּשְׁתַּמְּשִׁין בְּבַת קוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new, unrelated ruling in the same רבי שפטיה series.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may rely on a בת קול, learned from "ואזניך תשמענה דבר מאחריך".

steps.title: Limits on relying on a בת קול
steps.stepSummary: You may rely on the voice only if it is unusual (a man's voice in the city or a woman's voice in the field) and it repeats itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this applies when he heard a man's voice in the city or a woman's voice in the field, and when it said "yes, yes" or "no, no."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא limits the ruling of step 17. Not every voice counts. It has to be out of the ordinary, and it has to repeat its message.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Men were usually out in the fields and women usually in town. So a voice heard in the opposite place stands out and can be taken as a sign. The voice must also say its answer twice, "yes, yes" or "no, no," to show it is a clear message.

keyTerms.meaning: And this applies (only when...); introduces a limit
A man's voice in the city
A woman's voice in the field
Yes, yes
No, no

phrases.aramaic: וְהָנֵי מִילֵּי, דְּשָׁמַע קָל גַּבְרָא בְּמָתָא,
phrases.english: And this applies when he heard a man's voice in the city,
phrases.notes: Unusual, because men were usually in the fields.

phrases.english: or a woman's voice in the field.
phrases.notes: Unusual, because women were usually not in the fields.

phrases.english: And that is when it said: "Yes, yes"
and that is when it said: "No, no".

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the ruling of step 17 to specific conditions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A בת קול may be relied on only if the voice is unusual for its place and repeats its message.

steps.title: Reading Torah without a tune
steps.stepSummary: Someone who reads Torah without a tune or learns משנה without a melody is described by the פסוק "I gave them statutes that were not good."
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי שפטיה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Anyone who reads without a tune or learns without a melody, about him the פסוק says: "And I also gave them statutes that were not good."
steps.whatsHappening: The last ruling in the series. רבי יוחנן sharply criticizes reading Torah or learning משנה flatly, without a tune.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Learning with a tune shows love for the Torah and helps a person remember what he learned. Without it, the learning feels dry, as if the Torah were "חוקים לא טובים" to him. The פסוק from יחזקאל is applied to this person as a rebuke.

keyTerms.meaning: A pleasant tune (used for reading the Torah)
Learns or reviews (משנה)
Song or melody
Statutes that are not good

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן applies the harsh פסוק of 'חוקים לא טובים' to reading or learning without a tune. In the next step אביי objects to applying this פסוק to such a person.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁפַטְיָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Shefatya said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
Anyone who reads (the Torah) without a tune
or learns (משנה) without a melody,
about him the verse says:
"And I also gave them
statutes that were not good, etc."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁפַטְיָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן כׇּל הַקּוֹרֵא בְּלֹא נְעִימָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another independent ruling in the רבי שפטיה series.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Torah should be read and learned with a tune. Doing it without one earns the rebuke of "חוקים לא טובים".

steps.title: אביי objects: is a weak voice really that bad?
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks how a harsh פסוק could be applied to someone who simply cannot sing nicely.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי objected: Just because a person does not know how to make his voice sound pleasant, you apply to him the פסוק 'judgments by which they will not live'?!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks the previous teaching from Step 19. That teaching said that reading Torah or learning משנה without a tune fits the harsh פסוק 'חוקים לא טובים.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק speaks of laws that do not give life, which is a very severe description. אביי argues that this is far too strong for someone whose only problem is that he cannot sing well. Lacking a nice voice is not a real sin.

keyTerms.meaning: He strongly objected to it
To make the voice sweet or pleasant
You read (apply) the פסוק about him

phrases.english: Abaye strongly objected to this:
Just because he does not know how to make his voice pleasant —
you read about him 'judgments by which they will not live'?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the interpretation of the פסוק given in Step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: Applying 'משפטים לא יחיו בהם' to someone who reads without a tune
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The punishment is out of proportion. An unpleasant voice is not a sin worthy of such a harsh פסוק.

steps.title: The verse refers to scholars who quarrel
steps.stepSummary: אביי reapplies the פסוק, following רב משרשיא, to two תלמידי חכמים in one city who treat each other harshly in הלכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the פסוק follows רב משרשיא, who said: two תלמידי חכמים who live in the same city and are not pleasant to each other in הלכה, about them the פסוק says, 'And also I gave them statutes that were not good, and judgments by which they will not live.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי offers a better reading of the פסוק. It describes two scholars in the same city who fight with each other over הלכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem now is real wrongdoing, not a lack of musical talent. Scholars who quarrel turn Torah, which should give life, into a source of strife. That fits the harsh words of the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: Torah scholars
They are not pleasant (agreeable) to one another
Statutes that are not good

steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that fighting between scholars can make Torah itself feel 'not good.' The way people learn together matters.

phrases.english: Rather, it is like Rav Mesharshiya, who said:

phrases.aramaic: שְׁנֵי תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים הַיּוֹשְׁבִים בְּעִיר אַחַת
phrases.english: Two Torah scholars who live in one city

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין נוֹחִין זֶה אֶת זֶה בַּהֲלָכָה —
phrases.english: and are not pleasant to each other in halakha —
about them the verse says:

phrases.aramaic: ״וְגַם אֲנִי נָתַתִּי לָהֶם חוּקִּים לֹא טוֹבִים
phrases.english: 'And also I gave them statutes that were not good
and judgments by which they will not live.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves אביי's objection by reassigning the פסוק to a fitting case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק refers to one who reads without a tune.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק refers to תלמידי חכמים who quarrel over הלכה.
steps.whatToRemember: The harsh פסוק 'משפטים לא יחיו בהם' is applied to scholars who fight, not to someone who simply cannot sing.

steps.title: Holding a bare Torah scroll leads to being buried bare
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן teaches that whoever holds a ספר תורה directly with bare hands will be buried 'bare.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי פרנך said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Anyone who holds a ספר תורה bare will be buried bare.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רבי יוחנן warns against touching the parchment of a ספר תורה directly, with nothing in between.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The punishment matches the act: he held the Torah 'bare,' so he is buried 'bare.' What 'buried bare' means is not yet clear, and the next steps work it out.

keyTerms.meaning: One who holds
Bare, uncovered
Is buried

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי פַּרְנָךְ אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Parnakh said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
Anyone who holds a Torah scroll bare,
will be buried bare.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי פַּרְנָךְ אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new teaching about respect for the ספר תורה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Holding a ספר תורה directly with bare hands brings the punishment of being 'buried bare.'
steps.confusionAlert: 'ערום' here describes the ספר תורה being held without a covering. It does not describe the person being undressed.

steps.title: Can it really mean buried without clothing?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether he would literally be buried naked.
steps.simpleTranslation: Could it enter your mind that he is literally buried bare?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the literal meaning of 'buried bare.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Burying someone without clothing is a severe disgrace, and that cannot be the intended meaning. The words must mean something else.

keyTerms.meaning: Could it enter your mind? (this cannot be the meaning)

phrases.english: Bare — could it enter your mind?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the literal reading of Step 22.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A literal burial without clothes is unthinkable, so the words cannot mean that.

steps.title: Buried bare means without מצוות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reinterprets 'bare' as being without the merit of מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: he is buried bare, without מצוות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'bare' is a metaphor. He arrives at his burial empty of the merit of מצוות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'clothing' a person takes to the grave is his מצוות. Being 'bare' means losing that spiritual covering.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, say (read it this way)
Without מצוות

phrases.english: Rather, say:
he is buried bare, without מצוות.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 23 by reading 'bare' metaphorically.
steps.terutzMaskana: Buried without the merit of מצוות

steps.title: Would he really lose all his מצוות?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether he could really lose the merit of every מצוה he ever did.
steps.simpleTranslation: Could it enter your mind that he is buried without any מצוות at all?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer it just gave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Losing the merit of an entire lifetime of מצוות because of one mistake is far too harsh. The answer must be narrowed.

phrases.english: Without מצוות — could it enter your mind?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the explanation given in Step 24.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Forfeiting all of his מצוות is out of proportion to the act.

steps.title: אביי: he loses only that מצוה
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that he loses only the reward of the מצוה he did while holding the bare scroll.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, אביי said: he is buried bare, without that particular מצוה.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives the final, narrow meaning of 'buried bare.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only the reward for the specific מצוה he did, such as rolling or lifting the ספר תורה, is lost. He did it disrespectfully by touching the bare parchment, so it does not count for him.

keyTerms.meaning: That specific מצוה

steps.whatToRemember: Holding a ספר תורה with bare hands costs you the reward of the מצוה you were doing with it, but not all your other מצוות.

phrases.english: Rather, Abaye said:
he is buried bare, without that מצוה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves Step 25 by narrowing the loss to one מצוה.
steps.terutzMaskana: He loses only the reward of the מצוה done with the bare scroll.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basis for the practice of not touching the parchment of a ספר תורה directly.

steps.title: Roll the cloth, not the Torah scroll
steps.stepSummary: רבי ינאי teaches that when covering a ספר תורה, you wrap the cloth around the scroll instead of rolling the scroll into the cloth.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ינאי, son of רבי ינאי the Elder, said in the name of רבי ינאי the Great: It is better that the cloth be rolled, and the ספר תורה not be rolled.
steps.whatsHappening: A new practical teaching about respect for the ספר תורה. When you cover it, you should move the cloth, not the scroll.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Keeping the ספר תורה still and wrapping the מטפחת around it is more respectful than turning the holy scroll to fit the cloth. The scroll is not moved for the sake of its covering.

keyTerms.meaning: It is better
The cloth wrapper of a ספר תורה
Be rolled

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יַנַּאי בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יַנַּאי סָבָא
phrases.english: Rabbi Yannai, son of Rabbi Yannai the Elder, said
in the name of Rabbi Yannai the Great:
It is better that the cloth be rolled
and the Torah scroll not be rolled.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יַנַּאי בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יַנַּאי סָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of respect for the ספר תורה with a new practical rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wrap the מטפחת around the stationary ספר תורה rather than rolling the ספר תורה into the cloth.

steps.title: Each festival's reading is done in its own time
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings back the last line of the משנה. The פסוק 'וידבר משה את מועדי ה׳' teaches that each יום טוב's reading is done on that יום טוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'And משה declared the appointed times of ה׳ to the children of Israel.' The מצוה is to read each one of them at its own time.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting the final line of the משנה so it can say something about it. This sets up the ברייתא in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה learns from the word 'מועדי' (appointed times) that the Torah portion for each יום טוב belongs to its own day. You read about פסח on פסח, not all the festivals together and not at some other time.

keyTerms.meaning: The appointed times (festivals) of ה׳
Their מצוה, meaning how they are properly done
They read (in public, from the ספר תורה)
In its own time

phrases.english: "And Moses declared the appointed seasons of the Lord
phrases.notes: ויקרא כג:מד, the last פסוק of the festival chapter

phrases.english: to the children of Israel"
their מצוה is that they should read them
each and every one in its own time.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַיְדַבֵּר מֹשֶׁה אֶת מוֹעֲדֵי ה׳ אֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion of honoring a ספר תורה (רבי ינאי on wrapping it) and returns to the last line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each יום טוב's Torah reading is read on that יום טוב.

steps.title: משה set up studying each festival's laws on that festival
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that משה רבינו set up a practice: on each יום טוב, people should ask about and teach its own הלכות.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: משה set up for ישראל that they should ask questions and teach about the topic of the day. The הלכות of פסח are learned on פסח, the הלכות of עצרת on עצרת, and the הלכות of חג on חג.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that takes the משנה's idea one step further. Besides reading the Torah portion, people should also study and teach the day's הלכות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה spoke about the public reading (קריאה). The ברייתא adds learning (שואלין ודורשין): actually asking about and explaining the practical laws of that festival. So the idea of 'each one in its time' now covers both reading and studying, and this goes all the way back to a תקנה of משה רבינו.

keyTerms.meaning: He set up an enactment (a תקנה)
They ask questions and teach, explaining the הלכות
The topic of the day
The name חז״ל use for שבועות
'The festival,' the name חז״ל use for סוכות

steps.confusionAlert: In the language of חז״ל, 'עצרת' means שבועות (not שמיני עצרת), and plain 'חג' means סוכות.
steps.whatToRemember: Each יום טוב gets its own reading, and its own laws should be studied on it. This practice goes back to משה רבינו.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for teaching the הלכות of a festival on (and around) that festival. It is the basis of the well-known practice of learning a יום טוב's laws in its season.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
Moses enacted for the Jewish people
that they should ask and expound
about the subject of the day.
The laws of Passover, on Passover;
the laws of Shavuot, on Shavuot;
the laws of Sukkot, on Sukkot.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מֹשֶׁה תִּיקֵּן לָהֶם לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Widens the משנה's rule about reading each festival in its own time so that it also includes studying each festival's laws on it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משה set up a practice that each יום טוב's הלכות are asked about and taught on that יום טוב.

steps.title: הדרן: closing פרק בני העיר and מסכת מגילה
steps.stepSummary: The closing formula for פרק בני העיר, which also marks the end of מסכת מגילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, פרק בני העיר, and מסכת מגילה is now complete.
steps.whatsHappening: This is not an argument. It is the standard closing line said when finishing a פרק, and here it also ends the whole מסכת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'הדרן עלך' is a promise to come back and learn this פרק again. 'וסליקא לה' announces that the whole מסכת מגילה is finished.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you (said to the פרק)
It is completed
Tractate מגילה

phrases.english: We will return to you, chapter "The people of the city"
and this completes Tractate Megillah

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the פרק and the מסכת after the final ברייתא.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: פרק בני העיר and all of מסכת מגילה are complete.
